subject: Inde-Navarrette
research_tasks: Draft stage (2026-09-10) re-checked every video quote used in the draft against the research stage's cached YouTube auto-caption transcripts (S09, S10, S11, S12/S13, S14, S15, S16), and every web quote against a fresh verbatim HTML fetch (S02, S03, S04, S06, S07, S17, S19, S21, S22). Wording matches. Auto-captions are not audio: before publish, spot-check the load-bearing video lines against audio, especially S10 10:34-11:20 (Twitch deletion), S10 27:17-27:52 ('keep myself secure'), S11 35:48-36:01 ('chasing that high') and S09 20:24-21:10 (scream sessions).

S11 21:29-21:33 is garbled in captions ('went to Korean and go Mino can do this'). The draft paraphrases it only as 'she took the problem to Barker', then quotes Barker's clearly captioned reply. Confirm on audio that she addressed Barker there.

S13 attribution: the 'freaky Nikki' refusal (14:38-14:45) is attributed to Michael Johnston from turn order and content (he addresses 'you', and she pops her lips in response). Confirm visually. The Hot Ones lines at 02:21 ('Sometimes I just get anxious'), 04:57 ('the one thing I can control is taking off my jacket') and 12:09 ('do my parents proud') remain unattributed and are deliberately not used.
Alamo Drafthouse Q&A (S16) 15:16 'That was her idea, and it was brilliant' still has no speaker label and is not used.

Confirm on-screen credits for two names the draft uses: 'Sarah Cushing' (used by CBR 2021, Looper 2022 and Just Jared Jr. 2023; KryptonSite 2023 uses 'Cortez') and 'Cooper Tomlinson' as the actor who plays Ian (surname taken from the S16 video title; S09 gives only 'Cooper').

The draft calls Capstone 'the studio', following Barker's framing in S16. S29 describes Capstone as the production company behind several projects she appeared in. Confirm the preferred description before publish.
Birth date: the draft states only '2001' plus the third-party birthplace. March 3, 2001 appears only in third-party profiles (S01, S05); do not add a full birth date without a primary source.
Relationship status (rumored coverage of musician Nick Aiello as of 2026-09-10) remains unconfirmed by her. Do not add it to the body or FAQs.
Deadline (2026-08-31) reports an Obsession executive producer suing over profits. It does not involve Navarrette. Do not reference it or imply her involvement.
Sensitive: CBR 2021 (S19) has her saying she 'very personally' has an attachment to her character's mental-health arc. The draft omits it. Do not infer a diagnosis, an event or a causal wound.
Time-sensitive before publish: re-check the Obsession worldwide gross (S27) and the 'more than $500 million' as-of date.

sources.title: Inde Navarrette Wants To Prove 'Obsession' Isn't Just "Lightning In A Bottle"
sources.speaker: Inde Navarrette, interviewed by Lauren McCarthy (Nylon)
sources.locator: Corned-beef-at-the-deli profile; paragraphs on fame, auditions, privacy and dream projects
sources.excerpt: Strangers are now stopping her on the street... Her Instagram followers spiked to 2.2 million and counting. "I don't care how much I'm not sleeping, because I don't know if I'll get this opportunity again." / "Between Obsession and the film after that, I didn't work. I was walking dogs. I was streaming. I was doing a lot of these things to make money. I didn't have a lot of confidence because you just keep hearing no, and that can be debilitating." / "I just clock it. I don't want it to affect the way that I go about things, but I'm a very private person." / (Like Timothée Chalamet and Connor Storrie before her, old videos of Navarrette's streamer channel have been resurfaced...) / "I really want to prove that Obsession wasn't just lightning in a bottle... I also want to fall on my face publicly and have something that people don't like [but] maybe I do." She laughs. "So, I'm looking forward to that."
sources.context: In-person profile, about two months after release, over a half-pound of corned beef on rye at 11 a.m. The writer frames the privacy quote as being about unsolicited public attention. The resurfaced-streams observation is the writer's, not hers. Draft stage re-fetched the page and matched every quote verbatim (curly quotes normalized to straight).

sources.title: In Conversation With Inde Navarrette
sources.speaker: Inde Navarrette, interviewed by Jana Letonja; written by Anouk Woudt (Numero Netherlands)
sources.date: May 13 (year not displayed; content dates it to 2026)
sources.locator: Q&A: 'What drew you to the project?', 'How did working within the horror genre challenge you?', 'How does Obsession represent a turning point?'
sources.excerpt: I really wanted to transition into film, but to do it in a way that showed more of what I was capable of as an actress. Artistically, I felt like a boiling pot that kept being taken off the stove right before boiling over. Obsession was the perfect script for me to let it all out. / Horror was something I never thought I would be a part of. I am so deeply afraid of horror. / Obsession was the first time that I felt like I wasn't part of someone else's story.
sources.context: Release-week press Q&A. The written 'boiling pot' line is the draft's source for that image; she used a spoken version on GoldDerby (S11 03:07-03:18). The 'no control' line elsewhere in this Q&A is about playing Nikki and is not used as evidence of her own control needs. Draft stage re-fetched and matched wording verbatim.

sources.title: Obsession Star Inde Navarrette Explains What's Really Happening to Nikki (Collider Ladies Night)
sources.speaker: Inde Navarrette, interviewed by Perri Nemiroff
sources.locator: Timestamps: 01:42-01:59 ('feels like drugs... It's dopamine'), 04:36-04:42 (Gladiator), 06:02-06:10 (mom's advice), 08:07-08:45 (Superman & Lois as college), 09:45-10:15 (leaving the show), 13:59-14:13 (chemistry read with Cooper), 14:44-15:13 ('ugliness', felt seen, don't show that), 20:24-21:10 (shy, scream sessions, charades), 25:05-25:31 (alternate ending)
sources.excerpt: Funny enough, I didn't know how to scream. Whenever I met [Curry and] everybody, I was in a really shy place in my life... I said, "I don't know how to scream, and I'm feeling very shy." And he was like, "Okay, I'm going to schedule multiple days where it's just you and I, and then whenever you get comfortable with me, then we're going to do it in front of other people." And like, we played a charades game in order to kind of shock me out of it, and that created a really safe space... He did that where he would scream with me. And then he would stop and then I would stop. And he was like, "No, what are you doing? Come on, go go go go on." / Honestly, I kind of felt like it was a blessing, not necessarily in disguise, but kind of just right in front of my face... as soon as they were kind of like, "Dog, you're free." I was like, "Dude."... So, that was hard to hear cuz I miss everybody / my mom really instilled in me to um not take no until no's a for sure / how can I make him utterly uncomfortable right now? / And I felt seen, I felt heard... very similar to this film where whenever I read the script I was like, I know exactly how to play this... you're constantly told, "No, don't show that or don't be that or it's uncomfortable." / last minute we decided to change be like no she's a final girl she wouldn't do that / that feels like drugs. Feels great... It's dopamine.
sources.context: 30-minute spoiler interview on release weekend. Nemiroff frames the Superman & Lois exit as budget-driven before asking. The 'blessing' reframe is retrospective after Obsession's success. 'I felt seen, I felt heard' follows her praise of Chronology of Water and precedes her comparison to reading the Obsession script; the draft keeps that order and does not attribute the line to the script alone. Auto-caption renders Curry as 'Karyn'. Draft stage re-checked all quoted lines against the cached caption transcript.

sources.title: 'Obsession's Inde Navarrette on Fame, X-Men, Oscar Buzz, & What Video Games She's Playing (Up Next with Variety)
sources.speaker: Inde Navarrette, interviewed by Tiana (Variety)
sources.locator: Timestamps: 05:46-07:22 (family, Marine father, moving, divorce, Central Valley), 07:27-08:52 (strict dad, hit by a car, lenses, college), 10:33-11:34 (deleted Twitch streams, 'my fear was for nothing'), 11:41-12:44 (streaming origins, 'I don't think that far ahead', audience size), 14:30-14:46 (discerning, audience trust), 22:14-22:28 ('none of my business'), 23:55-24:25 (left high school early, Orangetheory), 25:24-27:07 (Gladiator, dance battles, 'jump off of a bridge', place to hide, Nikki stood up), 27:17-27:52 (control, 'keep myself secure'), 28:43-29:09 (Oscar safety net), 30:06-30:24 (sensitive to horror, community)
sources.excerpt: Oh, I like I deleted all of them just cuz I felt like I was I got scared and I was like, why moving into like a new chapter of my life? Like what if people saw that I switched and now they don't take me seriously or it was just a lot of I mean it's not based on fact, but it I just panicked and I deleted a lot of them... now seeing that people are so lovingly holding on to it my fear was for nothing, but I mean everybody gets scared, but I love love love streaming at that time and it also just helped me out with like financials / I don't think that far ahead... I love playing video games by myself. I'm not getting any work. I know that other people do this... I would max out at like 100. Um which was nice and like intimate. / whenever it comes to what I do have control over in order to keep myself secure um it'll be my drives. It'll be my music. It'll be my video games / there's a part of my brain that is um just kind of having a safety net of if it doesn't happen, it doesn't mean that I didn't do a good job / My dad's a Marine, so I grew up moving around a lot / Me, I was like new story, new place. / I left high school early to work at a coffee shop because headshots were really expensive and my mom couldn't afford them / I would never act in front of them. That to me felt like I would rather jump off of a bridge. / Nikki stood up for herself in so many different ways as Wish Nikki and real Nikki and I felt like that was something I needed to learn / the horror community has been the most welcoming out of anyone that I've ever been a part of and I don't ever want to leave that
sources.context: 33-minute solo podcast, the longest single-subject source; speaker attribution is unambiguous (one guest). The Twitch answer responds to 'Are the streams still up on Twitch?' 'I don't think that far ahead' answers whether she began streaming with a career in mind. The 'place to hide' phrase is one she credits to Milly Alcock. Captions render Superman & Lois as 'Superstore' and Obsession as 'Obsessed'. Draft stage re-checked every quoted line against the cached caption transcript.

sources.title: Inde Navarrette on 'Obsession' Oscar dreams, freaky stories, what happens to Nikki after the credits (GoldDerby Awards Magnet)
sources.speaker: Inde Navarrette, interviewed by Ethan Alter (GoldDerby)
sources.locator: Timestamps: 03:00-03:38 (boiling pot, worst audition), 05:13-05:32 (kept Nikki private), 09:21-09:31 (if that's what Curry said), 17:56-18:15 (sensitive, Curry as mirror), 21:05-21:38 (torn ACL, 'Danielle, hold it together', reverse the shot), 32:08-32:15 ('extremely validating'), 35:48-36:01 (chasing that high)
sources.excerpt: I felt as though it was the worst audition I had ever done. / I just needed to keep her private. I've really kept Nikki close to my chest. / I'm quite sensitive and so I didn't want to take anything home. So, I kind of used Curry as a mirror where I put full trust in him where I would show him the faces and he would tweak and whenever I heard, you know, that's perfect. No, keep it going. Keep it, keep it. That I loved / if that's what Curry said, then that's definitely what happened / Fun fact, I have a torn ACL... on the day we tried going backwards and tried going backwards and I was like Danielle, hold it together. You can do this... so he was like, "Wait, what if you go forwards and we reverse it? Like let's try that." And so obviously that's what we did in the film / I would be lying to you if I said that that's not a dream and that isn't extremely validating / Kind of chasing that high to challenge myself. I think obviously whenever you're really scared of something, but you really want to do it justice and do it correctly and then you get that high of uh accomplishing it and feeling proud of it.
sources.context: 37-minute awards-campaign podcast; incentive to present as serious and humble. The 'Curry relieved' detail is her account of Barker's words and is not used. The line between the self-coaching and Barker's reply (21:29-21:33) is garbled in captions. Draft stage re-checked quoted lines against the cached caption transcript.

sources.title: OBSESSION Q&A w/ Curry Barker, Inde Navarette, Michael Johnston, Cooper Tomlinson, Megan Lawless (Alamo Drafthouse)
sources.speaker: Curry Barker and Inde Navarrette (panel)
sources.locator: Timestamps: 16:17-16:24 ('up to me to make myself comfortable'), 22:57-23:32 (Barker on the ending)
sources.excerpt: Barker: what happened is we we were only going to shoot one take like I was just like it was kind a throw away, actually. Like, cuz we shot so many takes of the version that was in the script. And then, I was like, "Hey, listen, um Capstone really wants us to do a version where you live, so we're just going to do one one take one take where you live, and um whatever." And it Her performance was so crazy with the with the take where she lives, and so disturbing, um that I had people basically talk me into it and be like, "She has to live, dude. It's way crazier if she lives." / Navarrette: But there's some moments where it's just up to me to make myself comfortable.
sources.context: Post-screening panel. Barker's account of why the ending changed (studio-requested throwaway take, persuaded by her performance) differs in emphasis from hers in S09 (decided on the day: 'she's a final girl'); the draft attributes each version to its speaker. The video title supplies Cooper Tomlinson's surname. An unlabeled panelist says of the not-perceived idea 'That was her idea, and it was brilliant'; not used. Re-checked against the cached caption transcript at draft stage.

sources.title: TIFF 2025 Interview: Curry Barker on Crushing It in 'Obsession'
sources.speaker: Curry Barker, interviewed by Stephen Saito (Moveable Fest)
sources.locator: Answer to 'What sold you on Inde and Michael to play these characters?'
sources.excerpt: It was a really hard casting process because I was going for super-natural... some people were really good at the scary stuff, but they couldn't get the crazy stuff quite right, or they were really good at the crazy stuff, but they couldn't get the natural stuff quite right and that was a journey to find someone that could nail both those worlds, and Inde just nailed it.
sources.context: Pre-release festival interview, before the box-office run; the earliest director testimony and the least shaped by later success. Draft stage re-fetched and matched wording verbatim.

sources.title: Superman & Lois Interview: Inde Navarrette Breaks Down Sarah
sources.speaker: Inde Navarrette, interviewed by Meagan Damore (CBR)
sources.locator: Answers to 'How did you land the role of Sarah Cushing?' and 'Which aspect of Sarah's character do you relate to the most and why?'
sources.excerpt: I created this mindset with my mom when I was 13 about going into auditions... where if we don't get something, that's not what we're supposed to do... we'd go get lost, find dinner, come home, and by the time that we got home, if it was a bad audition -- like, I don't remember half of my auditions... So with that mindset, whenever I got old enough to drive myself, which was during the Superman & Lois auditions, I realized that I didn't have that distraction. I realized very quickly that I needed to kind of make a pact with myself of, "You know what? I'm going to give it 110%." That way, whenever I leave, there's no room for doubt, because doubt can really just weed its way in and just be a massive little B! / survival mode, almost, is what I like to call it, of going in, getting it done, and then leaving and letting it go once I leave the lot / With me feeling so uncomfortable with that nature, I brought my Zodiac book... from Aries all the way to Pisces, 12 signs... I wasn't talking to these girls, because I knew once I did, I would just want to be their friends / I love to think of myself as a very strong woman / I feel as though my stuff is my own and I'm very private about that.
sources.context: Pre-fame (series premiere) interview. Draft stage re-fetched the full page and matched every quoted line verbatim. The 'very personally' attachment line about the character's mental-health arc is deliberately omitted from the draft.

claims.claim: She arrived on Obsession 'in a really shy place' and told Barker she did not know how to scream.
claims.passage: "I was in a really shy place in my life." So she told Barker exactly that: "I said, 'I don't know how to scream, and I'm feeling very shy.'"
claims.inference: Her response to fear was to disclose it to a trusted authority. This is the opening instance of the name-the-fear, find-safety, commit sequence.
claims.alternative: Ordinary performance nerves handled by a good director. Shyness also fits Types 4, 5 or 9.

claims.claim: By her account, Barker scheduled private scream sessions before group ones, screamed alongside her, and had the cast play charades, which she said created a safe space.
claims.passage: By her account, Barker answered with a schedule. He booked days where it was just the two of them, and only once she was comfortable would she scream in front of anyone else. He screamed alongside her: "he would scream with me. And then he would stop and then I would stop. And he was like, 'No, what are you doing? Come on, go go go go on.'" He also got the cast playing charades, which she said "created a really safe space."
claims.inference: She accepted a structured, graduated exposure inside a trusted relationship. The schedule is her report of Barker's plan, not his own account.
claims.alternative: Standard directing technique for a nervous lead; it shows Barker's method as much as her motive.

claims.claim: In September 2026 she summarized the start of Obsession as charades 'because I was too scared to do shit'.
claims.passage: "The beginning of 'Obsession' was charades, because I was too scared to do shit."
claims.inference: Repeats the Collider account four months later in a different context, so the story is consistent across appearances.
claims.alternative: Comic game-show framing; transcript has no speaker labels (attributed from first-person repetition of S09).

claims.claim: Obsession was made for a reported $750,000.
claims.passage: The film she was too scared to start was made for a reported $750,000
claims.inference: Establishes the scale of the breakout. NBC News reports $750,000.
claims.alternative: The Numbers lists a $1,000,000 production budget; the draft attributes the figure as 'reported'.

claims.claim: Obsession had grossed more than $500 million worldwide by September 9, 2026.
claims.passage: had grossed more than $500 million worldwide by September 9, 2026
claims.inference: The Numbers lists $509,956,715 worldwide as of 2026-09-09. Establishes scale only.
claims.alternative: Gross is still moving; the as-of date keeps the statement true.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check The Numbers/Box Office Mojo before publish; update the figure and as-of date when the theatrical run ends.

claims.claim: Interpretation: her choices tend to follow a sequence of naming the fear, finding a person or structure that makes it safe, then committing fully.
claims.passage: She names the fear. She finds a person or a structure that makes it safe. Then she commits all the way.
claims.inference: Generalizes from the scream sessions (S09, S12), the chemistry read (S06), trust in Barker (S11) and the 2021 audition pact (S19).
claims.alternative: Several of these stories are standard press anecdotes; the sequence may reflect how actors narrate work rather than a personal motive.

claims.claim: Interpretation (type answer): her key discriminating behavior is securing against bad outcomes before they happen and borrowing certainty from trusted people.
claims.passage: The key clue is how she handles bad outcomes that have not happened yet: she secures against them early and borrows certainty from people she trusts.
claims.inference: Summarizes the Twitch deletion and Oscar safety net (S10) and the 'mirror' trust in Barker (S11) and scream sessions (S09).
claims.alternative: Type 7 reframing and impulsivity (C03, C12, C31) and Type 3 image management offer competing explanations of some of the same behavior.

claims.claim: She says she has been 'so sensitive' her whole life, especially towards horror movies, yet took a horror lead.
claims.passage: That fits a woman who says she has been "so sensitive" her whole life, "especially towards horror movies," and then took a horror lead
claims.inference: Moving toward a feared genre. S03 has the written version: 'I am so deeply afraid of horror.'
claims.alternative: 'Afraid of horror' is a common junket line, and her family watched horror when she was small (S14).

claims.claim: She was born Danielle Fabiola Navarrette in 2001, and profiles place her birth in Tucson, Arizona.
claims.passage: Navarrette was born Danielle Fabiola Navarrette in 2001; profiles place her birth in Tucson, Arizona
claims.inference: Birth name and year appear in several third-party profiles. Her self-address 'Danielle, hold it together' (S11) corroborates the first name; 'I just turned 25' in June 2026 (S14) fits the year. The draft attributes the birthplace to profiles.
claims.alternative: The exact day (March 3) appears only in third-party profiles and is omitted.

claims.claim: Her father is a Marine, and she grew up moving a lot.
claims.passage: "My dad's a Marine, so I grew up moving around a lot," she told Variety.
claims.inference: Her own statement (S10 06:10-06:14). Establishes the frequent relocation behind C03.
claims.alternative: None material. Details of his service are not stated.

claims.claim: Her parents divorced, and her mother raised the children mostly in California's Central Valley around Fresno, Visalia and Bakersfield.
claims.passage: Her parents divorced, and she says her mother raised the children mostly in California's Central Valley, around Fresno, Visalia and Bakersfield.
claims.inference: Her words: 'because my parents were divorced, my mom grew up or for the majority had us live in Fresno, like Visalia, Bakersfield' (S10 06:55-07:04).
claims.alternative: None material. The draft does not characterize the divorce beyond her statement.

claims.claim: She describes herself as the second-oldest in a large blended family of 'six or seven' children; Wikipedia lists four siblings.
claims.passage: She is the second-oldest in a large blended family, though she admits she loses count: "It's like six or seven."
claims.inference: She says 'second oldest of seven... It's like six or seven... they're kind of like split families' (S10 05:46-06:10). The discrepancy likely reflects step- and half-siblings; she mentions a stepmom (S04).
claims.alternative: The draft avoids a specific count beyond quoting her uncertainty.

claims.claim: Her family has an Australian side and a Mexican side.
claims.passage: The family has, as she put it on _Jimmy Kimmel Live_, an Australian side and a Mexican side
claims.inference: Her words: 'the Australian side of my family does not like horror movies at all, but the Mexican side does' (S14 07:04-07:09).
claims.alternative: Told for laughs on late-night TV; the draft uses only the heritage fact.

claims.claim: Unlike other military kids she knew, she says she liked moving: 'new story, new place'.
claims.passage: Other military kids she knew hated leaving their friends. "Me, I was like new story, new place."
claims.inference: Retrospective self-report (S10 06:25-06:50) showing childhood novelty tolerance. She adds that as an adult she has come to appreciate 'a small town mentality'.
claims.alternative: Counterevidence to a security-seeking reading; fits Type 7 novelty-seeking or simple adaptability. The draft counts it for the alternative.

claims.claim: Her nickname came from a childhood habit of insisting 'Mommy, I do', refusing her hairstylist mother's help with hair, bubbles and dressing.
claims.passage: "I would always say, 'Mommy, I do.' That's how I got my nickname, Inde, because I was very independent." Her mother, a hairstylist, offered to do her hair, blow her bubbles, help her dress. "Nope. Mommy, I do." Her mother's reply, in Navarrette's telling: "Okay. You're my first daughter. I would like to dress you."
claims.inference: An early, repeated insistence on doing things herself, told as her own origin story.
claims.alternative: Toddler autonomy is common to every type and does not discriminate; the draft says so.

claims.claim: At 13 she and her mother developed a shared audition mindset (if we don't get something, it wasn't meant to be) and made a day of each audition so bad ones faded.
claims.passage: "I created this mindset with my mom when I was 13 about going into auditions." The rule was that "if we don't get something, that's not what we're supposed to do." The two would make a whole day of each audition, so a bad one faded by the time they got home.
claims.inference: Pre-fame (2021) evidence that her early resilience was built inside a trusted relationship.
claims.alternative: A standard stage-parent narrative; it establishes influence, not motive.

claims.claim: Once she drove herself to auditions, she made a pact to give 110% so there would be 'no room for doubt'.
claims.passage: "I needed to kind of make a pact with myself of, 'You know what? I'm going to give it 110%.' That way, whenever I leave, there's no room for doubt, because doubt can really just weed its way in."
claims.inference: Names doubt as the enemy and sets up a pre-committed structure against it, a pre-fame instance of anticipatory self-securing.
claims.alternative: Generic effort talk common to ambitious performers; fits Type 3 as well.

claims.claim: She credits her mother with teaching her not to take no 'until no's a for sure'.
claims.passage: "my mom really instilled in me to um not take no until no's a for sure" (Collider)
claims.inference: Across 2021 (S19) and 2026 (S09) she credits a parent-installed script for rejection.
claims.alternative: Common inspirational framing; establishes influence, not motive.

claims.claim: She decided to act as a small child after watching Russell Crowe in Gladiator.
claims.passage: She has wanted to act since she was very small, after watching Russell Crowe in _Gladiator_.
claims.inference: Stable early vocation. She gives her age as 'like five' (S09) and 'like three' (S10); the draft says 'very small'.
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: She would dance-battle for her parents but never act in front of them.
claims.passage: "I would never act in front of them. That to me felt like I would rather jump off of a bridge."
claims.inference: Early privacy around the craft she most wanted, consistent with the later 'place to hide' framing (S10) and keeping Nikki private (S11).
claims.alternative: Ordinary childhood self-consciousness; told lightly on a podcast.

claims.claim: She left high school early to work at a coffee shop to pay for headshots, then did sales at an Orangetheory gym; her Marine father pushes education.
claims.passage: "I left high school early to work at a coffee shop because headshots were really expensive and my mom couldn't afford them," she said. Sales work at an Orangetheory gym followed. Her father, she says, "really really loves to push education."
claims.inference: A costly early choice that put the acting goal ahead of a conventional path (S10 23:55-24:25, 07:29-07:40).
claims.alternative: 'Left early' does not specify whether she finished by another route; the draft does not say 'dropped out'.

claims.claim: After a supporting role in the final season of 13 Reasons Why (2020), she joined The CW's Superman & Lois in 2021 as Sarah Cushing.
claims.passage: After a supporting role in the final season of _13 Reasons Why_ in 2020, Navarrette joined The CW's _Superman & Lois_ in 2021 as Sarah Cushing
claims.inference: Established filmography. S23 (June 2020) covers her role as Estela in the final season; S19 (March 2021) names the character Sarah Cushing.
claims.alternative: KryptonSite 2023 (S21) uses the surname Cortez; confirm credits.

claims.claim: She treated Superman & Lois as college; after being hit by a car she sat beside the DPs and asked about lenses.
claims.passage: With her father's emphasis on schooling in mind, she said, "I treated it like college." When she was hit by a car during production and couldn't walk between takes, she sat beside the directors of photography, who "always scared me," and started asking about lenses. "So even though I didn't have the opportunity to go to college I felt like I did."
claims.inference: Turns a constraint into structured learning, tied explicitly to her father's emphasis on education (S10 07:29-08:40; S09 08:11-08:24).
claims.alternative: A common 'set was my film school' narrative; also compatible with Type 5 or 7 curiosity. The accident details are only her account.

claims.claim: At her 2021 Superman & Lois screen test she wrote out the zodiac signs to hold focus, avoided talking to the other finalists, and called her approach 'survival mode'.
claims.passage: At her final screen test, surrounded by the other finalists, she felt "so uncomfortable" with the competition, so she brought a zodiac book and wrote out the signs "from Aries all the way to Pisces." She kept to herself on purpose: "I wasn't talking to these girls, because I knew once I did, I would just want to be their friends." She called the approach "survival mode": "going in, getting it done, and then leaving and letting it go."
claims.inference: Pre-fame example of managing pressure with a self-imposed structure; matches the 2026 'ran outside and... recalibrated' strategy (S09 02:20-02:25).
claims.alternative: Idiosyncratic nerves management; not type-specific.

claims.claim: In April 2023, even after James Gunn publicly backed the show, she withheld certainty about renewal until it was definitive.
claims.passage: even a public statement from DC's James Gunn did not settle it for her: "it's interesting in our industry, it's not a definitive, so we still have to wait for that answer."
claims.inference: A pre-fame, contemporaneous instance of withholding belief until an outcome is confirmed.
claims.alternative: Ordinary industry realism any working actor would voice. Weak on its own.

claims.claim: In June 2023 budget cuts ended her run as a Superman & Lois series regular, along with several castmates.
claims.passage: Two months later, budget cuts ended her run as a series regular, along with several castmates
claims.inference: Wikipedia reports she departed with six costars due to budget cuts in June 2023; Nemiroff frames the exit as budget-driven (S09 09:34-09:44).
claims.alternative: She returned in guest appearances; 'ended her run as a series regular' is the accurate scope.

claims.claim: In 2026 she described losing her series-regular role as a blessing and as being told 'Dog, you're free', while saying it was hard to hear because she missed the cast.
claims.passage: "Honestly, I kind of felt like it was a blessing, not necessarily in disguise, but kind of just right in front of my face," she told Collider. "As soon as they were kind of like, 'Dog, you're free.' I was like, 'Dude.'" She added that "that was hard to hear cuz I miss everybody."
claims.inference: Quick positive reframing of a loss, told in hindsight after Obsession's success. The contemporaneous 2023 reaction (S32) was not opened.
claims.alternative: A Type 7 marker (reframe toward freedom). The draft counts it for the alternative and labels the hindsight.

claims.claim: She describes her pre-Obsession career as a boiling pot repeatedly taken off the stove.
claims.passage: "Artistically, I felt like a boiling pot that kept being taken off the stove right before boiling over," she told Numero Netherlands in May 2026
claims.inference: Her own image of pent-up expression that circumstances kept interrupting (written in S03; spoken in S11 03:07-03:18).
claims.alternative: Supports Type 9 (self-suppression) or Type 4 as much as 6; also an actor's metaphor about small TV roles.

claims.claim: Her Obsession Zoom callback went badly; she says she was 'so shut off from my own emotions'.
claims.passage: "it was awful," she told Complex News in June 2026, as quoted by NME. "I think I was in a space personally where I was so shut off from my own emotions, and with Nikki, you need all of them."
claims.inference: Establishes a shut-down, fearful baseline before the decisive chemistry read (C58).
claims.alternative: A classic comeback-audition story shaped for press; fits many types.

claims.claim: She called the Zoom callback the worst audition she had ever done.
claims.passage: On GoldDerby's podcast she called it "the worst audition I had ever done."
claims.inference: Independent retelling in a second outlet (S11 03:33-03:38).
claims.alternative: Self-deprecating press framing.

claims.claim: She went into the chemistry read resolved to do everything she could.
claims.passage: "If I have this opportunity, I'm doing everything that I possibly can," she told Complex
claims.inference: Total commitment once the chance is finite; the 'commit all the way' step of C51.
claims.alternative: Ordinary last-chance determination; fits Types 3 and 8 as well.

claims.claim: At the chemistry read she locked eyes with Cooper Tomlinson and set out to make him uncomfortable.
claims.passage: In the room she locked eyes with Cooper Tomlinson, who would play Ian, and thought, "how can I make him utterly uncomfortable right now?"
claims.inference: Aggressive commitment in the moment (S09 13:59-14:13). Surname from the S16 panel title.
claims.alternative: A performance choice for a horror audition, not a personality disclosure.

claims.claim: Before release, Barker said few actors could do both the natural and the scary material, 'and Inde just nailed it'.
claims.passage: said actors could usually manage either the natural material or the frightening material, "and that was a journey to find someone that could nail both those worlds, and Inde just nailed it."
claims.inference: Named director testimony from September 2025, before the box-office run.
claims.alternative: A director praising his lead at a festival; not a personality assessment.

claims.claim: She kept her Nikki choices private from others on set.
claims.passage: "I just needed to keep her private. I've really kept Nikki close to my chest," she told GoldDerby.
claims.inference: Protects inner preparation from exposure until it is ready.
claims.alternative: A common actor technique for keeping reactions fresh; fits Type 4/5 privacy as well as 6.

claims.claim: Co-star Michael Johnston recalls asking her to show him the 'freaky Nikki' smile in advance and her refusing.
claims.passage: "When you did the smile, 'I'm your freaky Nikki,' remember I was like, 'Show me what you're going to do.' And you were like, 'No.'"
claims.inference: Second-person corroboration of C21.
claims.alternative: Friendly promotional context; speaker attribution inferred from turn order and needs visual confirmation.

claims.claim: She used Barker 'as a mirror' with 'full trust', loved his adjustments, and deferred to his memory of a disputed sequence.
claims.passage: "I'm quite sensitive and so I didn't want to take anything home. So, I kind of used Curry as a mirror where I put full trust in him," she told GoldDerby. She would show him faces, he would adjust them, and "whenever I heard, you know, that's perfect. No, keep it going. Keep it, keep it. That I loved." When an interviewer's question turned on Barker's memory of how a sequence came together, she deferred to it: "if that's what Curry said, then that's definitely what happened."
claims.inference: Borrowing certainty from a trusted authority to manage sensitivity (S11 17:56-18:15, 09:21-09:31). Counts against a Type 4 reading.
claims.alternative: Normal actor-director deference on an auteur's project; also fits a Type 9 merging reading. Barker credits her take with changing the ending (C36), so the deference is not total.

claims.claim: With a torn ACL, she coached herself ('Danielle, hold it together') through a backward-walk shot, then took the problem to Barker, whose fix (walk forward, reverse the footage) is in the film.
claims.passage: "Fun fact, I have a torn ACL," she told GoldDerby. When a scene called for Nikki to move backward, she tried and tried, coaching herself by her birth name: "Danielle, hold it together. You can do this." Then she took the problem to Barker, who asked, "Wait, what if you go forwards and we reverse it?" That is what ended up in the film.
claims.inference: Self-talk under a physical limit, then disclosure to the trusted director and acceptance of his workaround (S11 21:05-21:38).
claims.alternative: The line between self-coaching and Barker's reply is garbled in captions; 'took the problem to Barker' is a paraphrase. Physical workaround stories are ordinary production anecdotes.

claims.claim: The script ended with Nikki's death; Barker says Capstone requested one take where she lives and her performance persuaded him to use it.
claims.passage: The script ended with Nikki's death. Barker told an Alamo Drafthouse audience that the studio, Capstone, wanted "a version where you live," and he planned a single throwaway take. "Her performance was so crazy with the with the take where she lives, and so disturbing, um that I had people basically talk me into it."
claims.inference: Barker's account (S16 22:57-23:32) that her single take changed the ending. S09 corroborates that the scripted ending had Nikki die.
claims.alternative: Her account (C61) frames it as a same-day creative decision; the draft attributes each version to its speaker.

claims.claim: Navarrette recalls the ending change as a same-day decision because Nikki is 'a final girl'.
claims.passage: Navarrette remembers the change as a same-day creative call: "last minute we decided to change be like no she's a final girl she wouldn't do that."
claims.inference: Differs in emphasis from Barker's account (C36); both agree the ending changed on the strength of her take.
claims.alternative: Memory of a set decision two years earlier; she elsewhere defers to Barker's recollection (C23).

claims.claim: Barker says she brought a 'bro-y' sassiness to Nikki that he had not anticipated.
claims.passage: Barker has also said she brought "this like bro-y type of... sassiness to Nikki that I didn't anticipate"
claims.inference: Named director testimony about a tough, casual exterior he did not write (he wrote Nikki as a 'really sweet girl next door').
claims.alternative: Promotional praise; describes a performance choice rather than her personality.

claims.claim: Interpretation: for a Six, trust functions as infrastructure that enables risk; she protects her preparation, then hands final judgment to one trusted person.
claims.passage: For a Six, trust works like infrastructure: once it is in place, the risky work can begin.
claims.inference: Draws on C21, C22, C23, C48 and C60.
claims.alternative: Type 9 merging with an authority, or ordinary professional deference, could explain the same behavior.

claims.claim: After wrapping Obsession she went about a year and a half without another acting job.
claims.passage: After wrapping _Obsession_, Navarrette went about a year and a half without another acting job.
claims.inference: 'I didn't work for a year and a half after Obsession' (Complex, as quoted by NME).
claims.alternative: The figure is hers.

claims.claim: During the drought she walked dogs and streamed to make money and found repeated rejection debilitating.
claims.passage: "Between Obsession and the film after that, I didn't work. I was walking dogs. I was streaming. I was doing a lot of these things to make money," she told Nylon. "I didn't have a lot of confidence because you just keep hearing no, and that can be debilitating."
claims.inference: Establishes the cost and constraint behind the breakout; the same story appears in Complex (S06).
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: She streamed on a self-built gaming PC because she liked gaming alone and had no work, and she preferred a small, intimate audience.
claims.passage: The streaming ran on a gaming PC she built herself, Complex reported. "I love playing video games by myself. I'm not getting any work. I know that other people do this," she told Variety. She liked the small audience, which she called "nice and like intimate."
claims.inference: Streaming was both a financial fallback and something she enjoyed. The self-built PC is reported by Complex (S06) and HOLA! (S05); the rest is her account (S10 11:44-12:44).
claims.alternative: None material.

claims.claim: She deleted most of her Twitch streams because she got scared people would not take her seriously after switching to acting, admitting the fear was not based on fact.
claims.passage: "I deleted all of them just cuz I felt like I was I got scared." She explained the fear: "what if people saw that I switched and now they don't take me seriously." And she was candid that it was only a fear: "it's not based on fact, but it I just panicked and I deleted a lot of them."
claims.inference: Central discriminator (S10 10:34-10:55). Facing an imagined future judgment, she acted pre-emptively and at a cost, destroying an archive she loved that had helped pay bills, and named the act as fear-driven.
claims.alternative: A Type 3 image-management reading (protecting professional credibility). Against it, she volunteers the panic and calls the fear baseless. One retrospective episode, told lightly.

claims.claim: After fans preserved the clips she said her fear was for nothing, and that streaming had helped her financially.
claims.passage: "Now seeing that people are so lovingly holding on to it my fear was for nothing," she said, adding that she had loved streaming and that "it also just helped me out with like financials."
claims.inference: Establishes the cost of the deletion and her later reassessment (S10 11:10-11:30).
claims.alternative: Hindsight after a positive outcome.

claims.claim: Nylon observed that old videos from her streamer channel have resurfaced, as Timothée Chalamet's did.
claims.passage: Nylon noted that old videos from her streamer channel have resurfaced
claims.inference: An outside outlet's observation corroborating that the clips circulated.
claims.alternative: Writer's framing, not a quote from her.

claims.claim: Interpretation: her recurring move under threat is to secure against the worst case first, then check whether it was real, which is the Six sequence.
claims.passage: What she describes is the Six sequence: secure against the worst case first, then find out whether it was real.
claims.inference: Interprets self-reports across 2021-2026 and several interview contexts (C13, C15, C25, C24, C23, C48, C53). It names motive only as a hypothesis that fits repeated behavior.
claims.alternative: Type 7: novelty, reframing and 'high' language (C03, C12, C31, C69). Type 4: the wish to be seen (C34). Type 3: 'prove' language (C74). Most evidence comes from a single four-month promotional window for a film about losing control.

claims.claim: On Oscar buzz she keeps a 'safety net' against disappointment while admitting the conversation is extremely validating.
claims.passage: "there's a part of my brain that is um just kind of having a safety net of if it doesn't happen, it doesn't mean that I didn't do a good job." She did not pretend indifference. On GoldDerby she said she "would be lying to you if I said that that's not a dream and that isn't extremely validating."
claims.inference: Pre-committing against a feared disappointment before it happens, the same anticipatory structure as C15 (S10 28:55-29:09; S11 32:08-32:15).
claims.alternative: Media-trained modesty about awards is universal; weak alone.

claims.claim: She decompresses through things she can control, chosen 'in order to keep myself secure': drives, music, video games.
claims.passage: "whenever it comes to what I do have control over in order to keep myself secure um it'll be my drives. It'll be my music. It'll be my video games."
claims.inference: Explicit security vocabulary for emotional regulation (S10 27:36-27:52).
claims.alternative: Generic self-care; control language is inflated by the film's theme. The word 'secure' is the discriminating part.

claims.claim: She went skydiving and got her nipples pierced on her 18th birthday and says she loves getting random tattoos.
claims.passage: "On my 18th birthday, I went skydiving." Then: "I got my nipples pierced all in one day." She said she loves "getting random tattoos."
claims.inference: The strongest evidence for the Type 7 alternative (S14 03:07-03:15, 05:02-05:06).
claims.alternative: Strongest counterevidence to Type 6; told on late-night TV for laughs.

claims.claim: Asked whether she began streaming with a career in mind, she said she does not think that far ahead.
claims.passage: Asked whether she started streaming with a career in mind, she told Variety, "I don't think that far ahead."
claims.inference: Cuts against typical Six anticipation; listed as unexplained (S10 11:41-11:48).
claims.alternative: Offhand answer about a hobby; the draft treats it as counterevidence.

claims.claim: She describes a good audition as a high that feels like drugs: 'It's dopamine.'
claims.passage: She has described a good audition as a high that "feels like drugs," adding, "It's dopamine."
claims.inference: Stimulation language that supports the Type 7 alternative (S09 01:45-01:59).
claims.alternative: Common performer language about adrenaline.

claims.claim: Her interests range from gaming to a stated wish to write and direct.
claims.passage: a spread of enthusiasms from gaming to a wish to write and direct
claims.inference: 'write my own stuff and possibly direct one day' (S09 08:35-08:39); 'I want to direct one day' (S04). Breadth of interests supports the Type 7 alternative.
claims.alternative: Common actor ambitions.

claims.claim: She describes seeking the high of mastering something she is scared of.
claims.passage: "Kind of chasing that high to challenge myself. I think obviously whenever you're really scared of something, but you really want to do it justice and do it correctly and then you get that high of uh accomplishing it and feeling proud of it."
claims.inference: Her own statement of a counterphobic motive: the reward follows fear faced (S11 35:48-36:01). Echoes 2021 ('I often challenge myself daily', S19).
claims.alternative: Type 7 reading: 'high' language points to stimulation. Type 3 reading: the payoff is pride. The discriminator is that fear is named as the entry condition.

claims.claim: Talking about films that show a person's ugliness, she said she felt seen and heard, knew how to play the Obsession script, and is usually told not to show that side.
claims.passage: Talking about films that show a person's "ugliness," she told Collider, "I felt seen, I felt heard," and that with the _Obsession_ script she thought, "I know exactly how to play this." Showing that side is hard, she added, because "you're constantly told, 'No, don't show that or don't be that or it's uncomfortable.'"
claims.inference: Her strongest emotional-authenticity statements and the core evidence for the Type 4 alternative (S09 14:44-15:13). 'I felt seen, I felt heard' follows her praise of Chronology of Water; the draft keeps that context.
claims.alternative: Type 4 (desire to be seen in her full emotional truth). For the Six thesis, the relevant element is permission to show big emotion.

claims.claim: She calls the horror community the most welcoming she has been part of and says she never wants to leave it.
claims.passage: "has been the most welcoming out of anyone that I've ever been a part of and I don't ever want to leave that."
claims.inference: Belonging language rather than differentness, which counts against a Type 4 core (S10 30:15-30:24).
claims.alternative: Press-cycle gratitude toward a fan base.

claims.claim: She says playing Nikki taught her to stand up for herself, something she needed to learn.
claims.passage: "Nikki stood up for herself in so many different ways... I felt like that was something I needed to learn."
claims.inference: Argues against Type 8; compatible with a Nine finding a voice or a shy Six gaining nerve (S10 26:57-27:05).
claims.alternative: Type 9 or Type 4 identity-through-role readings.

claims.claim: In a 2023 slap scene she asked a castmate to slap her harder.
claims.passage: the actor who told a _Superman & Lois_ castmate "you've got to slap me harder" during a slap scene
claims.inference: A tough, physical self-presentation that could suggest Type 8 at face value; the draft weighs it against C33.
claims.alternative: Professional commitment to a scene's realism rather than a personality trait.

claims.claim: As Obsession broke out, strangers began stopping her and her Instagram following passed 2.2 million.
claims.passage: strangers began stopping her on the street and her Instagram following passed 2.2 million, Nylon reported
claims.inference: Context for the not-sleeping quote, reported by Nylon in July 2026.
claims.alternative: Follower counts move; the draft frames the figure historically, as reported at the breakout.

claims.claim: During the breakout she said she didn't care about lost sleep because she might not get this opportunity again.
claims.passage: "I don't care how much I'm not sleeping, because I don't know if I'll get this opportunity again."
claims.inference: Scarcity framing: success treated as possibly unrepeatable, driving overwork. Consistent with the anticipation in C15 and C25.
claims.alternative: A common first-breakout mindset; fits Type 3 or 7.

claims.claim: She has described herself as very private in 2021 and 2026, and handles strangers filming her by treating it as 'none of my business'.
claims.passage: In 2021 she told CBR, "I feel as though my stuff is my own and I'm very private about that." In 2026 she told Nylon, "I'm a very private person." Asked about strangers filming her in public, she described a deliberate narrowing of attention: "I kind of put it as like it's none of my business."
claims.inference: One of the few traits documented across time (2021 to 2026). The 'none of my business' strategy is a controlled narrowing of attention (S10 22:14-22:19).
claims.alternative: Privacy is not type-specific (common in 4, 5, 9) and is sensible for someone newly famous; the draft says so.

claims.claim: Echoing Milly Alcock, she describes acting as a place to hide and be another person.
claims.passage: borrowing an idea she credits to the actor Milly Alcock, as "a place to hide and to be another person."
claims.inference: Fits sensitivity and privacy around her craft (S10 26:29-26:44).
claims.alternative: A borrowed phrase; also fits Type 4 or 9.

claims.claim: She wants to be very discerning with next projects so as not to lose the audience's trust.
claims.passage: She wants to be "very discerning" with her next projects, she told Variety, because "I don't want to lose the audience's trust in me."
claims.inference: Trust is her stated currency with audiences, consistent with 6 (S10 14:30-14:46).
claims.alternative: Standard career-strategy talk during awards season.

claims.claim: She told Nylon she wants to prove Obsession wasn't lightning in a bottle and also wants to fall on her face publicly with something people dislike but she likes.
claims.passage: she said she wants to prove that _Obsession_ "wasn't just lightning in a bottle." Then she added: "I also want to fall on my face publicly and have something that people don't like [but] maybe I do." She laughed. "So, I'm looking forward to that."
claims.inference: A stated willingness to be disliked for something she loves, which cuts against the fear behind the Twitch deletion and against an image-first Type 3.
claims.alternative: The 'prove' language fits 3; willingness to be disliked fits 4; it is also press-tour bravado. The draft names these possibilities.

type_hypothesis.against: Several behaviors read more naturally as Type 7: she enjoyed childhood relocation ('new story, new place'), reframed losing her series-regular role as 'Dog, you're free', went skydiving and got her nipples pierced on the same day at 18, loves 'random tattoos', says 'I don't think that far ahead', and describes a good audition as a high that 'feels like drugs... It's dopamine'. Her most emotional statements ('I felt seen, I felt heard'; being told 'don't show that') fit Type 4. Her 'prove' and 'extremely validating' language fits Type 3. Much of the evidence is self-report from May-September 2026 promotion, where humble-fearless framing is rewarded, and the role she was promoting is about losing control, which inflates control vocabulary. The Hot Ones anxiety lines are situational and their speakers are unconfirmed, so they are not used.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: A Type 7 reading explains her novelty tolerance in childhood moves, fast positive reframes of loss, same-day stunts at 18, 'random' tattoos, breadth of interests (gaming, streaming, voice acting, writing and directing), irreverent talk-show persona, and the 'high'/'dopamine' vocabulary. On this reading the fear talk is a junket convention and the Twitch deletion a one-off impulse.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What she does when a bad outcome is only possible, not yet real. A 7 reframes toward options and holds on to sources of pleasure; a 6 acts pre-emptively to secure against the worst case and borrows certainty from trusted people. Her clearest unforced case is deleting her own Twitch archive, which she loved and which had helped pay bills, because people might not 'take me seriously', while conceding 'it's not based on fact... I just panicked' (Variety, 2026-07-31). The same structure recurs: an Oscar 'safety net' set up before any nomination; rituals chosen 'in order to keep myself secure'; disclosing shyness to Barker and accepting a staged safe container before screaming (Collider 2026-05-16; Hot Ones 2026-09-08); 'used Curry as a mirror where I put full trust in him' (GoldDerby 2026-06-12); and, pre-fame, a 2021 pact against doubt and a 2023 refusal to believe a renewal until it was 'definitive'. Her 'high' is explicitly conditional on fear first ('whenever you're really scared of something... you get that high of accomplishing it'), which is counterphobic mastery rather than novelty for its own sake. Against Type 4, she hands her read of the character to the director and speaks of belonging (horror community 'I don't ever want to leave that'), not of being different.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The genuine enjoyment of constant childhood moves and the same-day skydive and piercing are not well explained by a security motive; the skydive can be read either way, but the piercing and 'random tattoos' fit stimulation better. 'I don't think that far ahead' sits against typical Six anticipation. The 'boiling pot' image and her need to learn assertiveness through Nikki could indicate a Type 9 pattern of self-suppression. Lifelong privacy fits 4, 5 and 9 as well. There is little independent testimony from outside the Obsession promotional circle (no family, Superman & Lois colleagues or pre-2020 accounts), and the pre-fame record (2020-2023) is thin.
